extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, engineers, factory owners, industrialists, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and political‑economic principles for designing, applying, and evaluating machinery and manufactures — covering mechanical sources of advantage, factory organisation, division of labour, cost accounting, and the interplay of science and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOURCES OF THE ADVANTAGES ARISING FROM MACHINERY AND MANUFACTURES
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter I heading and opening thesis: the advantages of machinery arise principally from additions to human power, economy of human time, and conversion of common/low‑value substances into valuable products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains mechanical additions (wind, water, steam, tools), economy of time (e.g., using gunpowder for blasting), and use of low‑value materials (goldbeaters' skin, horny refuse, old tin ware). Includes experimental evidence (Redelet's block‑of‑stone experiment showing rollers/soap massively reduce force required) and illustrative anecdotes (diamond cutting tool improvement). Use this criterion to judge whether a proposed machine/manufacture increases effective power, saves time, or valorises cheap inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACCUMULATING POWER
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter II: when work requires more force than can be produced in the time allowed — methods to accumulate or store power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses fly‑wheels, rolling‑iron, pile‑engines, and anecdotal examples (punching plate‑iron). Use to evaluate designs that store/accumulate energy to meet intermittent high loads; assess components like flywheels, gearing, and energy reservoirs for correctness and adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: REGULATING POWER
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter III: means to regulate delivered power to make machine output uniform and controllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers mechanical governors (steam‑engine governor), uniform fuel supply, consuming smoke, vane regulation by air resistance, striking clocks, cataracts used in mine engines. Guidance includes recognising appropriate regulation mechanisms for application (speed governors, feed regulators, timing devices) and evaluating their reliability under operating conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: INCREASE AND DIMINUTION OF VELOCITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter IV: effects of velocity changes on fatigue, efficiency, and mechanical processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates human muscular fatigue vs magnitude, optimal loads for porters, examples in spinning (hand vs wheel) and winding machines, tilt‑hammer driven by spring, scythe‑making. Use criterion when assessing operating speeds of machines and ergonomics of human‑machine interaction; consider tradeoffs between speed, accuracy, and worker fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: EXTENDING TIME OF ACTION OF FORCES
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter V: methods to prolong the action of forces to perform work over time (e.g., clocks, jacks, automatons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses watches and clocks, common jack, automatons; notes uses in physical experiments and agitating chemical solutions. Apply when a process needs long, continuous, or slow action — evaluate mechanisms (escapements, cams, jacks) for consistency and suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAVING TIME IN NATURAL OPERATIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter VI: applying processes and machinery to accelerate natural or chemical/physical operations (e.g., tanning, bleaching, evaporation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tanning, impregnating timber with tar, bleaching linen, accelerating evaporation of brine, deepening rivers. Use to judge whether proposed machinery accelerates inherently slow natural processes and whether such acceleration is practical and economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: EXERTING FORCES TOO GREAT FOR HUMAN POWER, AND EXECUTING OPERATIONS TOO DELICATE FOR HUMAN TOUCH
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter VII: substituting machines where forces exceed human capability or where precision exceeds human touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers difficulties of synchronous action by many people, working with red‑hot rivets, spinning cotton, steamboats, damping paper for bank notes. Use this criterion to justify mechanisation where magnitude or delicacy of forces demands machines; evaluate machine suitability for delicate or heavy tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: REGISTERING OPERATIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter VIII: necessity and methods for measuring, registering, and counting machine outputs and inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses pedometers, counting machines for carriages, steam‑engine indicators, calico measuring machines, tell‑tales, instruments for measuring liquor drawn/from casks, gas‑ and water‑meters, instruments for averaging fluctuating forces, barometer clocks, alarms, repeating clocks/watches. Guidance: evaluate metering and recording devices for accuracy, tamper‑resistance, calibration, and suitability for process control and accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: ECONOMY OF MATERIALS EMPLOYED
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter IX: techniques and principles to minimise material waste and optimise use of raw material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include cutting trees into planks, printing‑ink experiments. Evaluate processes to reduce scrap, improve yield, and choose cutting/processing methods that lower material cost per unit without harming quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDENTITY AND ACCURACY OF WORK
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter X: when work is of the same kind it should be identical; when different kinds, consider accuracy requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics: turning tops of boxes in lathes, accuracy from tools and turning. Use to assess tolerancing, interchangeability, and whether machine processes produce consistent identical outputs or acceptable variation when differing outputs are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPYING (METHODS AND APPLICATIONS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XI: extensive classification and principles of copying processes (printing from cavities/surfaces, casting, moulding, stamping, punching, drawing, cutting, copying with altered dimensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed treatment: copper‑plate printing, engraving on steel, music printing, calico printing from cylinders, stencilling, lithography, register printing; casting in metals, plaster, wax; moulding bricks, tiles, embossed china; swaging, chain making, screw‑cutting, pentergraph, rose engine, die copying, etc. Guidance: evaluate which copying method best suits a product, considering fidelity, throughput, tooling cost, scalability, and susceptibility to forgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: METHOD OF OBSERVING MANUFACTORIES
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XII: how to study and record manufacturing processes — skeletons, general inquiries, and process skeleton for each operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides templates/skeletons for observing each process, suggesting what to note. Use as a checklist for factory visits: record process steps, inputs, outputs, timings, tooling, labour, and failure points to enable analysis and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN MAKING AND MANUFACTURING
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XIII: conceptual distinction between individual making and organised manufacturing operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explores how manufacturing integrates multiple processes, division of labour, scale, and organisation differently from simple making. Use to decide whether a product should be produced by hand/artisan methods or by organised manufacture based on volume, standardisation, and cost structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFLUENCE OF VERIFICATION ON PRICE
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XIV: how verification/inspection, standards, and ability to test quality influence price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers verification of sugar, tea, flour; doctoring feed; difficulty of distinguishing 'single press' lace; watches; measures of linen drapery; apothecaries and druggists; effect of number of proprietors on price; examples like oil of cajeput and ice. Guidance: assess how verifiability of quality affects market price, incentives for adulteration, and requirements for inspection/certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: INFLUENCE OF DURABILITY ON PRICE
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XV: the effect of product durability on its monetary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses degrees of durability for paper, pens, precious stones, tables, chairs, mirrors. Use to evaluate price relative to lifespan — durable goods often command higher price per unit or different market expectations; factor durability into cost accounting and marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRICE AS MEASURED BY MONEY
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XVI: factors affecting money price, lists of historical prices, and elements causing price alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains lists of prices for various years, table of elements of alteration, causes of price changes, middle‑men influence. Guidance: use historical price data and element tables to analyze price movements and decompose influences (raw material, labour, duties, distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: RAW MATERIALS (NATURE AND COST)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XVII: characteristics of raw materials and their role in manufacture, including price comparison and country differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses gold/silver leaf, Venetian gold chains, watch‑spring, tables of price of raw material and labour across France, price of bar‑iron in various countries. Guidance: evaluate sourcing, comparative cost stages, and how raw material quality/price impacts final cost and manufacturability.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIVISION OF LABOUR (CAUSES AND ADVANTAGES)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XVIII: causes of advantages from division of labour, time to learn an art, time lost changing occupations, skill from repetition, and tools' contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers nail‑making, bank note signing, pin‑making with English/French/American comparisons, tables of costs, principle of repeated practice increasing skill, and new principle of advantage of division. Use to evaluate process segmentation, workstation design, training costs, and when to apply further division or automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIVISION OF MENTAL LABOUR
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XIX: organising intellectual labour (e.g., calculation) across people and machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses large tables of logarithms, performing arithmetical calculations by machinery, explanation of mathematical principles, illustrative clocks. Use to assess centralisation vs distribution of calculation tasks, and where mechanised calculation (computing machines) increases productivity and reduces error.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEPARATE COST OF EACH PROCESS IN A MANUFACTURE
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XX: accounting for cost per process/stage and analysing value added at each stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparative value of cotton of Java at different manufacture stages, statement of expense of printing the present volume, observations on costs, effect of duties on paper, advertisement charges. Guidance: perform stage‑wise cost accounting to identify cost drivers, margins at each step, and where improvements yield greatest benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: CAUSES AND CONSEQUENCES OF LARGE FACTORIES
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXI: why large factories form, transport of materials, continuous vs shift operation, maintenance, steam application, gas lighting, accounting departments, workers' profit share, effects on raw produce economy, middle‑men, and confidence/trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses factory scale economics (e.g., machines working 8 vs 24 hours requiring multiple crews), organisational departments, benefits of profit sharing to workers, examples from Cornish mines, horn economy, sending agents abroad, parliamentary report excerpts. Use to evaluate optimal scale, labour scheduling, supply chain, and governance incentives for large establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: POSITION OF GREAT FACTORIES
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXII: siting factories relative to transport, fuel, water, and cheap conveyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises locating on lines of cheap conveyance, fuel and water access; examples include Mississippi and steamboats, facilitating markets and removal/relocation. Use to judge site selection, logistics costs, and relocation feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: OVER‑MANUFACTURING
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXIII: causes, periodicity and remedies for over‑production and its effects on markets and capital allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers periodical over‑manufacturing, effects when lacking large establishments, compensation systems, remedies like diminished production or lower costs, and reallocation of capital. Use as criterion to monitor supply vs demand, inventory levels, and systemic market responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: INQUIRIES PREVIOUS TO COMMENCING ANY MANUFACTORY
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXIV: pre‑start investigations — capital, tooling, supply of raw material, probable demand, tolls and transport effects, time to returns, probable opposition to new manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: evaluate cost of tools/machines, raw material availability, market demand forecasting, regulatory/toll impacts (e.g., tolls on steam‑carriages), road draught calculations, and time to return on investment. Use as a pre‑investment checklist and feasibility study template.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONTRIVING MACHINERY (DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT PRACTICES)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXV: practical advice on inventing mechanical contrivances, drawings, experiments, causes of failure, importance of stiffness in framing and of good workmanship, repeat experiments and cost considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions that combinations of machinery are rare and recommends making drawings to determine movements, trying experiments for physical/chemical circumstances, repeating trials at intervals, using good workmanship for testing, and estimating expense of new machines. Use to appraise R&D methodology, prototyping practices, and risk factors in machine development.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPER CIRCUMSTANCES FOR THE APPLICATION OF MACHINERY
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXVI: when to apply machinery (large quantities, high accuracy, economy of time), and consideration of competition between machine and hand labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: newspapers, The Times, conveyance of letters, steam‑carriages, diving vessels. Use to decide suitability of mechanisation: prefer machines when many identical items are needed, where accuracy matters, or where time saving is decisive; consider social and economic impacts on hand labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: DURATION OF MACHINERY
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXVII: lifespan and depreciation of machinery and effects of improvements, hire/letting of machines and power, and unexpected market effects of machine availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes engines producing power last long, improvements increase production, watches' ages, letting machines for hire, changes in rent of stocking frames, letting stamps/dies/steam power. Use to evaluate capital lifespan, depreciation strategy, leasing models, and how technology improvements affect asset value.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMBINATION AMONGST MASTERS OR WORKMEN AGAINST EACH OTHER
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXVIII: rules and effects of combinations/unions among masters or workmen, their objectives and consequences, and examples (gun barrels, coal/iron works, truck system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes factory rules, larger societies of workers, causes of expense due to fear of combination, reasons for factory removal, truck system and payment of wages in goods. Use to assess industrial relations, unionisation risks, regulatory responses, and wage/payment system impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMBINATIONS OF MASTERS AGAINST THE PUBLIC
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXIX: cartels/monopolies among masters (e.g., gas, water companies, coal‑owners, booksellers), their effects and remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gas and water companies, coal‑owners, booksellers, combinations affecting reviews and profits. Discusses remedies. Use for antitrust considerations, market power assessment, and policy remedies to protect consumers/competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: EFFECT OF TAXES AND LOCAL RESTRICTIONS ON MANUFACTURES
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXX: how taxes, excise regulations, duties, monopolies/bounties, and local restrictions affect manufacturing (e.g., taxes on paper/windows, excise rules, insurance on smuggling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes effects of duties, bounties, removal of monopolies (bobbin‑net trade), patent/copyright expenses, limited partnerships. Use to evaluate fiscal/regulatory impacts on costs, incentives for smuggling or circumvention, and optimal policy environment for industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: EXPORTATION OF MACHINERY
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXXI: arguments for and against exporting machinery, impact on competition, and impossibility of preventing export while any export permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses competition between manufacturers in poor vs rich countries, impossibility of preventing exportation, makers' incentives to supply home vs foreign markets, effect on internal communications and railroads (Manchester example). Use to weigh IP/trade policy, competitiveness, and global diffusion of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: FUTURE PROSPECTS OF MANUFACTURES AS CONNECTED WITH SCIENCE
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XXXII: the union of theory and practice; fostering science within manufacturing; societal institutions and the effect of public opinion; chemical discoveries arising in manufacturing; and long‑term outlook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for closer links between science and manufacture, benefits of scientific societies/associations, examples of discoveries by manufacturers (iodine, bromine), chemistry concentrating quinia, and potential sources of power (tides, geothermal). Use to judge R&D strategy, human capital development, and long‑term industrial policy linking science and manufacturing.
